opus-5.5.text:
I think judgment and priors end up doing a lot more of the work than people often like to admit. There's a tempting picture where you take a benchmark, plot performance over time or against compute, fit a curve, extrapolate, and the data tells you when some capability arrives. In practice, the data rarely pins things down that tightly.

Part of it is that benchmarks are a weak proxy for what we actually care about. A benchmark measures performance on a fixed, fairly narrow distribution of tasks, and what we want to know is something like: when will these systems be able to do economically meaningful work, or automate a large fraction of research, or substantially accelerate the economy? Getting from "the model scores 90% on this test" to "the model can do this job" requires a model of how the benchmark relates to the real-world task. That isn't something the benchmark itself can tell you. You have to bring it in from outside, and that's where judgment comes in.

Then there's the extrapolation problem. Benchmarks saturate, often quickly. Many follow an S-shaped curve: near zero for a while, a rapid rise, then a plateau near the ceiling. If you're in the early flat part, you can't easily tell when the rise starts. If you're in the steep part, you can't easily tell where it levels off or whether the ceiling reflects the benchmark's limits or the model's. So the same data is consistent with very different forecasts, and what separates them is largely your prior about how capabilities scale and how hard the remaining parts of the task are.

There's also a recurring pattern: models do surprisingly well on benchmarks people thought were hard, and are still surprisingly bad at things that seem easy, like long-horizon agency, coherence over many steps, or adapting reliably to messy environments. That's a version of Moravec's paradox. If you just look at the headline benchmark numbers, you'd conclude we're very close to systems that can do most cognitive work. If you look at how these systems perform when deployed, the picture is more mixed. Reconciling those requires judgment about which signals are more informative.

So my view is that you can't avoid priors. The question is whether you're explicit about them. I'd rather someone say, "here's my prior on how much compute it takes to reach a given capability, here's how I'm updating on this benchmark trend, and here's why I think the benchmark is or isn't representative," than present a curve fit as if it were objective. The curve fit has priors baked in through the choice of functional form, the choice of benchmark, and the assumption that the trend continues. Those are judgment calls too, just hidden ones.

I also think people should be humbler about how much any single benchmark result should move them. A lot of the discourse swings wildly whenever a new model posts a big number on some eval. Often the right update is smaller than it feels, because the benchmark was already close to saturating, or there's contamination, or the result doesn't transfer to the broader capability you care about. Over time, the more reliable signal comes from aggregating across many benchmarks and, increasingly, from real-world usage and economic impact, because that's ultimately what we're trying to forecast.

r001.rationale: It says benchmark data rarely pins forecasts down and that different forecasts from the same data depend largely on priors about capability scaling.

r002.rationale: It notes that benchmark trends may level off or saturate and that assuming a trend continues is a judgment call, making extrapolation uncertain.

fable-5.1.text:
I think judgment ends up doing a lot more of the work than people like to admit. The naive picture is that you have a benchmark, you have a trend line, you extrapolate the trend line, and then you read off when the benchmark saturates and that tells you when some capability arrives. And every step of that has a judgment call hidden inside it.

The first one is what the benchmark is actually measuring. When a model goes from, say, forty percent to eighty percent on some coding benchmark, you have to ask whether that corresponds to the thing you care about, which is usually something like "can this system do economically useful work without a human babysitting it." Benchmarks are constructed to be gradeable, which means they tend to be short, self-contained, and have a clear right answer. Real tasks mostly aren't like that. So you need a prior about how much saturating the benchmark transfers to the messy version of the task, and that prior comes from your model of what the system is actually doing, not from the benchmark itself.

The second judgment call is which trend you're extrapolating. On most of these benchmarks, if you fit a curve to the last two years you get a very different answer than if you fit it to the last five, and both of those are defensible choices. The data is noisy, the benchmarks keep getting replaced as they saturate, and you're often stitching together things that were never designed to be comparable. People sometimes treat the trend line as if it's a measurement, but really it's a summary of the past plus a strong assumption that whatever drove the past keeps driving the future at the same rate. That assumption is where your priors about compute scaling, algorithmic progress, data availability, and so on all get smuggled in.

And then the third thing is just base rates. If you look at the history of forecasting technology from leading indicators, there's a pretty consistent pattern where the indicator moves fast and the downstream impact lags by a lot more than people expected. So even when I believe a benchmark trend, I try to apply a fairly strong discount about how quickly that turns into something you'd notice in the economy. That's a prior I hold with some confidence, and it's not something you can derive from the benchmark data at all.

So my honest view is that benchmarks are useful mostly as a check on your judgment rather than a replacement for it. If I think some capability is five years away and the benchmarks saturate next year, that should make me nervous and go back and look at my reasoning. But if the benchmark alone is the argument, I'd want to know what the person's model is of why that number means what they say it means. Usually when you push on that, the disagreement turns out to be about the priors, and the benchmark was just where it surfaced.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark data is noisy and incomplete, and that extrapolation depends on assumptions and priors about scaling, algorithms, data, and transfer to real tasks.

r002.rationale: It notes that extrapolation assumes whatever drove past trends will keep driving the future at the same rate, identifying uncertainty in that assumption as a limitation.

astra-6.text:
I think judgment enters much earlier than people sometimes realize. A benchmark gives you a measurement, but it doesn’t tell you how to translate that measurement into a forecast. You have to decide whether it captures the capability you care about, whether improvements are likely to continue, and whether performance will transfer to tasks outside the benchmark. Those are all judgments.

Priors matter because the evidence is often compatible with several different stories. If a model suddenly improves on a benchmark, is that a broadly useful capability emerging, or is it getting better at a relatively narrow class of tasks? People with different prior expectations can look at the same result and update differently, without either of them necessarily being irrational.

What I would want is for those assumptions to be explicit. What did you expect before seeing the result? How surprising was the result under your view? And what would make you change your mind? You can also ask how much your forecast changes if you use a different, reasonable prior. If it changes dramatically, then you should acknowledge that the benchmark hasn’t settled the question.

So I see benchmarks as useful constraints on judgment. They can rule out some views and make others more plausible. But there’s still a substantial inferential step between a benchmark score and a claim about what AI will be able to do in the world.

r001.rationale: It says the evidence can fit several stories and that people with different priors can interpret the same result differently, conveying why forecasts depend on priors when evidence is inconclusive.

r002.rationale: It questions whether benchmark improvements will continue, but does not identify uncertainty about future trend breaks as a limitation of extrapolating performance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think judgment is unavoidable here. A benchmark gives you an observation, but it doesn’t tell you how to interpret that observation. If a model does well, is that because it has acquired a general capability, because the tasks are particularly suited to its training, or because the evaluation gives it a lot of help? Those explanations imply different things about what happens next.

Your priors matter especially when you extrapolate. You might have a fairly smooth trend in benchmark performance, but translating that into a forecast about doing economically useful work requires assumptions about how representative the benchmark is. And people can agree on all the measured results while disagreeing substantially about those assumptions.

So I’d try to make the judgment explicit. What did you expect before seeing the result? How surprising is the result under different views of AI progress? And how much should it change your forecast? Ideally, you also check whether your interpretation predicts performance on other tasks. The point is to let the evidence constrain your judgment, while recognizing that a benchmark score alone isn’t a forecast.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark observations are insufficient to interpret capability and that extrapolation depends on assumptions and priors, conveying why limited evidence makes forecasts more dependent on them.

r002.rationale: It notes that a smooth benchmark trend does not by itself forecast future outcomes, but does not identify uncertainty about future trend breaks.
